messages.subject: Re: MultiBUGS benchmarks on different computers
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nathan,

thanks for that summary. This made me look at MultiBUGS again. I had looked at it a while back and ran into a range of issues. After spending another day with it I still have the same issues. While simple occupancy models run fine, I keep getting a range of trap errors with more complex occupancy and SCR models, all of which run fine in JAGS. Errors change depending on the initial values provided but none of the errors point to a specific issue. The most persistent one is Trap 101   (invariant violated). Models compile fine and initialize but throw an error after the MPImsimp initiation. No idea what is going wrong.

If you (or anyone else) has any advice on how to avoid some of these issues that would be great. I have several projects where I could really use MulitBUGS to reduce run times and I have the hardware to take advantage of it.

Thanks,

Mathias

On 28.09.2019 02:00, Kery Marc wrote:

> Thanks for the interesting report, Nathan.
>
> Makes me think about buying some new stuff...
>
> Regards  --- Marc
> From: hmec...@googlegroups.com [hmec...@googlegroups.com] on behalf of Nathan B [twa...@gmail.com]
> Sent: 27 September 2019 21:23
> To: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology
> Subject: MultiBUGS benchmarks on different computers
>
> I have recently been using MultiBUGS to run some closed-population modeling code from the Kery and Schaub book that I've modified to work across multiple occasions. Just to give you a feel for the size of the dataset, there are 15 occasions with a total of 13,832 individuals (including the augmented "fake" ones). I also estimate the effect of size class (3 categories) on detection. I was wondering which computer I had available to me would give me the fastest run times.
>
> I recorded the run time for the first 1000 samples on three different machines using MultiBUGS. For each machine, I distributed MultiBUGS to run on all possible threads. So for example, my work desktop is a 4 core machine with Hyperthreading = 8 threads. The machines represent different ages of CPU technology and a variety of thread counts. My work desktop is a relatively new machine (about a year old). The server I had access to was around five years old or so, and is pretty slow on single-threaded basis (around 3.5 Ghz boost), but has 40 available threads. Finally I compared these to a new Ryzen 3900x computer that runs 24 threads, but at a slightly lower freq that the Intel (about 4.1 GHz).
>
> 1) Intel desktop- Intel Xeon W-2125 (4 cores/8 threads; 4.4Ghz boost).                Run time: 122s.  CPU usage: 99%
> 2) Server- Intel E5-2687Wv3 x2 (10C/20T x 2 CPUs=40 threads; 3.5Ghz boost). Run time 84s.     CPU usage 75%
> 3) Ryzen desktop- AMD Ryzen 3900x (12C/24T ~ 4.1GHz boost).                        Run time 50s.     CPU usage 91%
>
> As you can see, running MultiBUGS on a machine with lots of threads substantially improves the run time, and it pays to have newer tech...big surprise there :) . The 5-year old 40 core machine (~$10k) was well outpaced by a consumer desktop (~$1k). Also note that CPU usage varies. I've noticed this between models as well. I have a growth model that does not seem to take advantage of the full CPU power when distributed across multiple cores, no matter which computer I used, but was still faster than running single-threaded. Here are those results:
>
>     Xeon Server (2x 10/20T): 105s. CPU usage 28%
>     Xeon desktop (W-2125 4/8T): 85s CPU usage 47%
>     Ryzen desktop (3900x 12/24T): 40s CPU usage 31%
>
> In this case, with the lower CPU usage, the Xeon desktop now outpaces the Server, presumably because the thread count matters less and the cpu speed comes into play more. But the Ryzen chip with fewer threads than the server and lower clock than the Intel desktop still blows both of them out of the water.
>
> I really look forward to the development of MultiBUGS and newer, faster, cheaper multi-core processors.
>
> Nathan

Nathan
